newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: Guatemala signs peace accord to end 36-year war.
newsitem.headline: Guatemala signs peace accord to end 36-year war.

text.p: Guatemala's government and leftist rebels prepared to sign a historic peace treaty on Sunday ending a war that has remained a stubborn reminder of the conflicts that racked Central America in the 1980s.

On the eve of the ceremony destined to change the face of a country stained by decades of bloodshed, commanders of the Guatemalan National Revolutionary Unit (URNG) rebels arrived in the capital brimming with enthusiasm after years in exile.

Their exuberant supporters, including young students, unionists and Indian peasant groups, greeted the rebel commanders at Guatemala City airport as returning heroes, waving banners, URNG flags and cheering wildly.
It was an unprecedented show of public support for the rebels in a nation where once civilians were dragged from their beds, tortured and shot simply for being suspected leftists.
Some 140,000 people were killed or "disappeared" during the 36-year conflict, most in the Cold War years of the 1980s.

But rebel leaders said the days when Guatemala was a quagmire of massacres, coup d'etats and military dictatorships were now buried in the past and they indicated little doubt they were committed to a peaceful future.

"We've come to stay in Guatemala, to continue to fight for the most profound aspirations of this country for which we have given a large part of our lives," said URNG commander Pablo Monsanto, who first fled into exile in the mid-1960s and has only returned clandestinely to the country since.
Indian leader Rigoberta Menchu, who won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1992, wiped tears from her eyes as she hugged the arriving commanders.

Menchu told reporters the peace accords contained the most significant government recognition of Indian rights ever adopted in Latin America, including programmes to bring equality to Guatemala's mostly poor indigenous majority.

"A great majority of the soldiers in the army are Indian. The majority of the members of the URNG are Indian. And we can't forget that the great majority of the (war's) victims are Indian," said Menchu.

The speed with which President Alvaro Arzu, with only one year in office, brought an end to the war has won him broad acclaim, and the peace ceremony was due to be attended by the heads of state of many Latin American countries and Spain.

Dozens of foreign dignitaries, including Boutros Boutros-Ghali, outgoing secretary-general of the United Nations, which brokered the peace accords, were scheduled to attend the peace signing at 5 p.m. (2300 GMT).

Among ordinary Guatemalans scepticism fostered by years of terror and broken promises still runs deep. Enthusiasm was muted at an overnight celebration in front of the National Palace, where the signing was slated to take place.

"This is a diplomatic circus. So much death, so much anguish cannot just be stopped by signing a piece of paper," said Rolando Grajeda, a university worker who brought his wife and children to the central plaza.

The hard-won peace treaty follows five years of off-and-on peace negotiations and contains 10 separate agreements covering everything from health and education to huge cuts in military personnel and details on the disarming of the rebels.
But much of its success hinges on foreign loans and donations, and Arzu's government has spent months on an international campaign to round up funds.
Rebel troops, who number 1,700 and are still hidden in camps in the mountains, were expected to stay out of Guatemala City and watch the peace treaty on television.
In the new year they will turn in their arms under the scrutiny of international peace monitors, and many plan to work as organisers in the political party the URNG plans to form.
